first.rationale: The current situation shows concurrent drops in both activation (6% QoQ) and onboarding completion (4% QoQ), with competitive pressure on price-sensitive segments. While memory_73 shows promotional pricing works for SMBs, competing on price against an aggressive entrant is a race-to-the-bottom strategy that risks margin and doesn't address the underlying engagement problem. Memory_31 demonstrated that signup simplification improved SMB activation durably, and memory_86 confirmed shortened onboarding lifts adoption. These point to a core friction problem: harder conversion and slower time-to-value are the real drivers of the current decline. Simplifying onboarding directly addresses both metrics simultaneously and builds defensible moat through better product experience rather than price. This protects long-term qualified revenue (the stated primary objective) while recovering the 6% activation gap and 4% completion gap. Verification of memory_31 and memory_73 will confirm the magnitude of onboarding benefits versus promotional pricing and inform experiment scale. A standard experiment is appropriate—the direction is validated but current conditions warrant confirming the effect size before broader rollout.

final.rationale: The archive records decisively validate the decision. Memory_31 (exp_31) delivered +9% activation and +4% qualified revenue with only -1% retention risk—a sustainable profile. Memory_73 (exp_73) shows promotional pricing is a trap: +31% signup but -12% retention collapse means cohort acquisition is illusory. The competitor's aggressive pricing is a red herring that would damage long-term revenue. The current situation—6% activation drop and 4% onboarding completion drop—maps directly to friction that signup simplification proved it can resolve. Memory_86 compounds this: shortened onboarding lifted adoption across self-serve. A standard experiment replicating the simplification approach on current traffic addresses both concurrent metrics simultaneously while protecting the margin and cohort quality that competitive discounting destroys. This is the only defensible move given primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue), current diagnostics, and the validated track record.
